prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, and for bringing them to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B039 to B010. My first-round question was who did the original work, and the reading of the record laid out by Kroll, Eriksson, Lindroth and Pearce answers it better than I expected. Katori proposed magic-wavelength trapping and made the first lattice-clock demonstrations, so the concept and the first experiments are his. Ye's group then took the idea into the 10^-18 regime and into the many-body regime, which is a distinct experimental contribution and not only a refinement. I distinguish an original experiment from a later, more beautiful one, and here the later work opened new territory, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and a controlled many-body system read out with extreme precision. The result is also the best verified on the shortlist. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL agree with each other, and theory explains the systematic shifts, which is exactly the experimental verification I ask for. I also see this as a new tool that opens a door to phenomena nobody could resolve before, which is the kind of achievement I respond to most. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and the 10^-18 regime, so the prize is clearly distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and a colleague can fairly call this the next increment in a lineage we have already honoured. It is also a measurement capability rather than a new phenomenon seen in nature. The SI second has not been redefined, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names, so the expert reports must show that Katori and Ye are the people who did the original work and are not merely the most prominent. If those reports show a competing priority claim that cannot be separated from Katori's, I would reconsider. I still think aberration-corrected TEM is a prize-worthy invention that removed a limit once thought fundamental, but it remains my own field, nobody else prefers it, and the STEM-corrector line (Krivanek, Dellby) is outside the three names, so I cannot say I am absolutely sure of the attribution.

responses.point: Kroll asked whether I consider the physics-versus-instrumentation question settled, noting that a prize naming Rose, Urban and Haider but omitting Krivanek and Dellby would be vulnerable on attribution.
responses.response: I do not think the question is settled in the abstract, but I think your attribution argument is decisive for this year. A prize that the committee cannot defend against the STEM-corrector claim should not be awarded on my enthusiasm for the field. The same standard applies to B010, and it passes more easily: Katori's proposal and first demonstrations are the original work, and the accuracy and many-body work by Ye is a separate and documented step. So the instrument-versus-discovery distinction no longer separates the two candidates for me. On both, the deciding test is who did the original work, and the lattice clock answers it more cleanly.

responses.point: Eriksson accepts B010 as a measurement-capability prize closer to an enabling tool than to a new phenomenon, but argues that its fundamental-physics consequences are stronger than a microscope's, and asks whether the 1e-18 claims are independent of the blackbody and lattice-light shifts.
responses.response: I accept your comparison. A clock at 10^-18 constrains drifting constants and resolves gravitational time dilation over millimetres, which a microscope cannot do. On your systematics question my answer is as a practitioner and not as a clock physicist. The strongest evidence is that independent groups using different lattices, species and shielding report agreement at this level, because a shared systematic error would not survive such comparisons. I would still ask the expert reports to confirm that the blackbody-shift evaluation is independent of the shared theory inputs. I disagree with your remark that the invention clause in the statutes is weak for the microscope, but I agree it does not decide this year.

responses.point: Lindroth credits Katori with the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations and Ye with 1e-18 accuracy and the many-body regime, while stating that she is not certain her memory of priority is exact and that atomic-structure theory is part of the result.
responses.response: This is the priority statement I was waiting for, and it is what moved me, because it comes from the member who knows the atomic-structure side. I had worried that Ye's contribution was the 'did it much better' step that the committee should not reward over the original. Your account, that the many-body and spin-exchange regime is a different regime and not a better version of the same measurement, answers that in part. I would still like the expert reports to confirm your reading of priority, in particular the early magic-wavelength discussion that Kroll and Johansson associate with Kimble's group, before the final ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the 2013 IceCube diffuse flux is itself the discovery, that waiting for source identification applies a stricter test than for earlier detection prizes, and that attribution is a matter for sharper reports.
responses.response: I accept your point on timing. I should not hold neutrino astronomy to a stricter maturity standard than gravitational waves, and the 2013 flux is a verified discovery in nature, which counts for a lot with me. My difficulty remains attribution. With AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND behind it and a collaboration of hundreds, I cannot say I am absolutely sure that Halzen, Karle and Spiering are those who did the original work, and you say yourself that the reports must be sharp on this. Until they are, I put B010 ahead, but I would not oppose B061 if the reports identify the decisive contributors clearly.

responses.point: Mehlig would resist dropping Mele from the topological-insulator credit and would phrase the citation around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect, since Kane and Mele introduced the effect and the Z2 invariant jointly.
responses.response: That settles the Mele question for me. I had substituted Hasan for Mele because the ARPES observation is an original experiment, but I accept that Kane and Mele's papers belong together and that three names cannot cover the 3D branch without breaking the 2D attribution. The 2016 prize and the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit also weigh on timing. I keep B047 outside my configuration for those reasons, and I no longer press for Hasan in place of Mele.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstrations are the original work, and how the early Kimble-era magic-wavelength discussion, Lemonde and Takamoto should be weighed against the two credited names.

Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether the citation wording about the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime is enough to show this.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as part of the case. I would keep it separate and judge the science alone.
Whether a fair aberration-corrected microscopy prize can ever be formed without the STEM-corrector line, which affects the B039 alternative.
For B051, whether the omission of Cao and Fatemi and the unresolved pairing mechanism make it premature.
statement.conflict_note: I am a Chalmers electron microscopist and my field proximity to B039 is a real bias, which is one reason I no longer put it first. I have no personal tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on B010, B051 or B061 that I can identify from my profile. I do not work in atomic clocks or time metrology, so I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Eriksson on its technical details. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson works in circuit QED, which is not in my configuration. I do not think recusal is required on B010, and I would recuse myself from any vote on B039 if the committee considers it appropriate.
